note: This is the best time of year to see Beautyberry in its full purple. Like a Dr Seuss plant!
area: Near Office and around Cypress Pond
quick_hits: Around the beginning of September, tight clusters of vivid purple fruit appear directly around the stems. At Palma Sola, that is when Beautyberry suddenly seems to be everywhere.
American Beautyberry is a Florida native. Ours grow around Cypress Pond and the office, and some appear to have seeded themselves into new spots.
The fruit is edible, though fresh Beautyberries are tart and not especially flavorful; they are more often made into jelly, with a lot of sugar.

note: Great shot of these blooming by Sofia, one of our high school volunteers! The mass planting outside the office is at times unruly, so we enjoy them now while we can.
quick_hits: The showy orange bracts are not flowers — they are modified leaves. The actual flowers are the small structures tucked inside them. The bracts last for weeks after the true flowers have finished.

The curved bract shape is a near-exact match for a hummingbird bill. Plant and bird have been shaping each other through coevolution. In its native range, hummingbirds become territorial over specific heliconia plants, defending them as a private nectar supply.

note: Rhonda took a nice shot of this guy eating some fruit, which is generally frowned upon, but this meal was already on the ground.
quick_hits: Males are bright red with a pointed crest and black face mask; females are warm buff-brown with red tinges. Both carry the same stout orange-red bill.
Both sexes sing. In many North American songbirds only the male does.
That heavy conical bill is a seed-cracker, opening tough seeds many birds cannot manage.

note: Jenny caught this beast as she walked to the Galleria and took this great shot of its coloring. Beautiful and creepy at the same time.
quick_hits: One of Florida's largest grasshoppers, an adult Eastern Lubber can reach about three inches long.
The wings are too small for sustained flight. Adults mostly walk and climb, with only short hops when disturbed.
The black, yellow, orange or red coloration is a warning. Lubbers contain defensive chemicals and can release a foul-smelling froth when threatened.

note: To the left of the pavilion, between the butterfly garden and the rare fruit area is this hidden gem. Full glory of yellow right now!
quick_hits: Long chains of yellow flowers hang from the branches in late spring and early summer, briefly turning an otherwise inconspicuous tree into something much easier to spot.
The dark cylindrical pods that follow can reach about two feet long and stay on the tree through the winter.
Break open a mature pod and it isn't one long hollow tube: the seeds sit in a row, separated by partitions, with dark pulp packed around them.

note: The Geiger Tree can be found in a couple spots. In the middle of the hibiscus garden in the field behind the office. Or in the welcome island. You passed in on the way in.
quick_hits: Clusters of orange-red flowers can appear again and again through the warm season.
Rub a leaf and you have the other name for it — sandpaper leaf. Both surfaces are genuinely rough.
Pale, wrinkled fruits follow the flowers.

note: Our team planted a new tree in September to replace the fallen baobab from the storms of past years. We also lost a rainbow eucalyptus near the cactus garden, so this is a welcome back of sorts!
quick_hits: The bark is not dyed or treated. Every color on that trunk follows a predictable sequence: the outer bark peels away to reveal bright green inner bark, which then shifts through blue and purple, deepens into orange and red, and finally fades to brown — at which point the cycle starts over. Different patches are always at different stages, which is why the whole trunk reads as a mosaic.
